Rylee Schultz’s cover photo and the story of her first hunt were submitted by her mother on her
behalf. As her mother tells the story behind the photo, this was my daughter’s first deer on her very
first year of hunting in 2020. Her Dad and I were super proud of her when she dropped him with
one shot. Just before this moment she was very skeptical if she ever was going to get a deer. The
week before, we saw a spike at 20 yards and she completely missed. She was bummed, but we kept
telling her that hunting isn’t just about the harvest. It’s the overall hunting experience.
Yes, hunting can be difficult and things happen from time to time. In this case it happened for a rea-
son! On Oct. 26, 2020, we saw this beautiful buck. He wasn’t very smart considering he was follow-
ing a doe. He didn’t seem to mind us getting Rylee’s tripod set up. He leisurely kept on walking. At
this moment Rylee was shaking, and I whispered to her, “Breathe and focus on your shot placement.”
She had a few open shots but there was tall brush and made it difficult. Dad told her, “The moment
he stops with no brush, squeeze the trigger.”
The buck finally stopped at about 70 yards out, and she
squeezed that trigger. He immediately dropped! We both started tearing up with excitement and
she said, “I can’t believe that just happened!”

A juvenile ram is defined as a male bighorn sheep having at least one "unbroomed" horn that does not extend past an imaginary line beginning at the point on the animal's forehead
where the front of the horn base adjoins the skull, and continuing downwards and in a posterior direction through the posterior edge of the eye. All reference points are based on viewing

thus shortening its length and disrupting its natural taper.
